claims.text: NbTaTiV is a refractory BCC high-entropy alloy.
Toughness retention in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys is governed by the predominance of mobile edge dislocations over screw dislocations.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can increase the fraction of edge dislocations.
Increasing the fraction of edge dislocations will produce more uniform plastic deformation.
Increasing the fraction of edge dislocations will improve toughness retention.
Conventionally hot-worked NbTaTiV has a mixed population of screw and edge dislocations.
Rapid quenching after hot working can lock in the altered dislocation structure.
Mobile edge dislocations permit easier dislocation glide.
Easier glide by mobile edge dislocations facilitates uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation delays crack initiation.
Screw dislocations inhibit uniform deformation under high stress and temperature.
A shift toward edge-dominated dislocation networks improves toughness retention.
Relative to conventionally processed NbTaTiV, the modified alloy will have higher fracture toughness.
Relative to conventionally processed NbTaTiV, the modified alloy will have higher ductility.
The modified alloy will exhibit a quantifiable increase in the fraction of edge dislocations.
The proposed relationship should apply to refractory BCC high-entropy alloys processed between 900 and 1200 °C under controlled strain-rate conditions.
The proposed relationship may not apply outside the specified processing window or in alloy systems with substantially different dislocation mechanisms.
